BMW Is Paying Insane Money To Get 8,000 Employees Gone by the End of 2027
12 photos
Photo: BMW
BMW just closed the counter on its German layoff program, the reason being too many takers. The Munich-based automaker needs 8,000 white collars out the door by the end of 2027, so it emailed severance offers to tens of thousands of staff. Roughly 40,000 people logged in to see what their exit was actually worth, and curiously enough, the internal HR portal folded within hours.
As per German publication Handelsblatt, the fix landed the next day, and the applications kept stacking higher and higher. A few days later, BMW stopped taking new ones altogether so it could process the queue. When a cost-cutting program develops a waiting list, chances are the company does not have a persuasion problem anymore. Instead, a triage problem arises.
What's pulling those applicants in line? As reported by Handelsblatt, which is citing insiders, individual dealers are clearing 650,000 euros. That puts BMW above Mercedes and Volkswagen. The latter, which is the largest German and European manufacturer of them all, topped out near 405,000 euros two years ago, devoid of an early-bird premium.
Over at Merc, long-serving team leads were paid around half a million euros last year. BMW seemingly read the market, then bolted on the so-called Turbo Bonus for anyone who agrees to take the early exit. The offer itself hands subject employees two doors out, specifically March 31 of 2027 or October 31 of 2027. The early doors pay extra, and the program dies at the end of that October no matter what happens until then.
Handelsblatt understands the math runs on an individual basis under uniform principles. BMW , however, understandably refused to comment on concrete figures. The manufacturer's generosity should not be viewed as a poisoned chalice, but as cold-blooded bookkeeping. Cutting those 8,000 positions by the end of next year will bank the company around one billion euros per year from 2028.
Photo: BMW Simply put, writing comically large checks now helps BMW write fewer payroll checks in the near future. Of course, there are a few ways to take the money offered by the Munich-based manufacturer.
Employees are offered installments, one lump sum, part of the negotiated sum into the company's pension pot, part into a direct insurance, or any blend of the aforementioned. BMW is also happy to include a well-wishing qualified reference letter, if the applicant asks for one.
Turning 55 before the program ends, the employee counts as a retiree for certain extras, employee conditions on new and used cars included. The company car clause is especially interesting. Anyone leaving can buy their last service car in the month their contract ends, and senior pay grades can walk out with two such vehicles. Looking at the bigger picture, it's no wonder BMW had to make quitting irresistible during these incredibly difficult of times.
The hurry behind all of this comes from the most recent of sales charts, with China being the automaker's biggest oof right now. BMW sales in the PRC dropped by almost 25 percent in the last quarter, while growth in Europe and the US could not plug the China-shaped hole in the Q3 2026 sales report.
Via // Handelsblatt
